rows.why: The internal decisions and workflows AI output drives, who the staff users are and the settings it is used in are identified and documented.
Requirements for the AI in internal workflows (accuracy needed, confidentiality, who may use it for what) are gathered from the staff and process owners who use it.
Staff are told what the AI cannot reliably do and how its output may be used and checked before it drives an internal decision.
rows.review_reason: Empty cis_refs although LLM-14.9 (role-specific training) supports telling staff what the AI cannot do and how to check its output.

rows.why: The benefits expected from AI in each internal workflow are examined with the staff who use it, so over-reliance is weighed against what the AI really adds.
The costs of wrong output acted on in internal decisions (HR, finance, approvals, operations) are examined against the organisation's risk tolerance.
The decisions and workflows the AI may drive internally are scoped, with those it may not drive stated.
Human review of AI output before it becomes an internal decision or action is defined, assessed and documented, so staff do not over-rely on it.
The likelihood and size of harm from wrong or misused AI output in internal workflows, including insider misuse, are identified and documented.
The AI's performance is measured on the real HR, finance and approval cases it is used for, not only in generic tests.
How the AI is behaving inside internal workflows in production, including drift and unusual use by staff, is monitored.
Each internal workflow fails safely, falling back to manual handling or a hold, when the AI is wrong or beyond its knowledge limits.
Who used the AI, on what, and which decisions relied on its output are logged so internal use can be traced and accounted for.
Staff can interpret the AI output in its context, with the reasoning or basis needed to judge it before acting.
Bias in AI-driven internal decisions, such as HR and approvals, is evaluated and the results documented.
Staff and those affected by an internal decision can report problems with AI output and appeal or challenge the outcome.
rows.review_reason: LLM-17.3 is a security-incident reporting process, not a way for staff or affected people to report AI output problems or appeal; weak support for this row.

rows.why: Domain experts in the business function confirm that the AI is performing as intended in the internal workflow it supports.
A decision is made on whether the AI achieves its purpose in each internal workflow and whether that use should continue.
Working controls limit what the AI may do in internal decisions (business rules, limits on what output is accepted, how staff and AI share the task).
rows.review_reason: Why (business rules, limits on accepted output, how staff and AI share the task) repeats MAP 3.3 (scope of decisions) and MAP 3.5 (human review) in different words.

rows.why: Procedures exist to respond to and recover from a decision made on wrong AI output or insider misuse once it is found.
Responsibility and a means exist to switch off or override the AI in an internal workflow when its outcomes depart from intended use.
Incidents and errors from AI-driven internal decisions are reported, tracked, communicated to those affected and reviewed.

notes.reason: Bias in HR and approval decisions harms the employees or candidates affected; the area's impacts (process, data) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: HR and finance data handled through the AI (employee records, insider access) carries privacy risk that nothing in the rows examines for this area.

rows.why: The customer-facing application's intended purpose, the public users and settings it serves, and the harm it could do to customers are understood and documented.
Requirements for the customer-facing application (privacy of customers, safe answers, abuse resistance) are elicited and built into its design.
What the customer-facing AI does not know or must not answer is documented and told to customers and staff.
The benefits to customers of the customer-facing AI are examined and documented so they can be weighed against the harms of wrong or leaked answers.
The scope of what the customer-facing application may answer or do is specified and limited to what its capability and context support.
rows.review_reason: Scope of what the application may answer or do largely repeats MAP 2.2 (what it must not answer, told to customers); merge into one check or separate clearly.

rows.why: Human oversight of the customer-facing AI (review, escalation to a person, override) is defined, assessed and documented.
Likelihood, magnitude and cost of harm from public attacks and bad or leaked answers reaching customers are assessed from expected use and past incidents.
Answer quality and safety of the customer-facing application are measured under conditions like real customer use, not only in the lab.
The customer-facing application's behaviour in production is monitored for wrong answers, abuse patterns and drift.
The customer-facing AI is shown to give valid, reliable answers, and the conditions beyond which its answers cannot be relied on are documented.
rows.review_reason: Repeats MAP 2.2 (documented limits beyond which answers cannot be relied on), and answer validity and reliability with no attacker belongs to the Output area.

rows.why: The customer-facing AI is tested for unsafe or harmful answers and shown to fail safely when pushed beyond its limits.
Security of the public-facing AI against prompt injection, jailbreaks and abuse is tested, for example by red-teaming, and results are documented.
Customer interactions with the AI are logged with enough detail to review errors, abuse and leaks and to hold someone accountable.
Privacy risk of the customer-facing AI, including leaking one customer's or the organisation's data in answers, is examined and documented.
Customers can report problems with the AI's answers and appeal outcomes, and this feedback feeds the evaluation of the application.
rows.review_reason: Folded MAP 5.2 is not fully asked: the why covers problem reports and appeals but not the practices and people for regular engagement or feedback on positive and unanticipated impacts; ask it fully or make MAP 5.2 its own row.

rows.why: A determination is made, using monitoring and test results, whether the customer-facing AI meets its purpose and should stay in front of customers.
Controls on the customer-facing AI (input and output filtering, guardrails, rate limits, data minimisation) are in place and applied to sustain its safe operation.
rows.review_reason: Outcome is sustaining the value of the deployed system, but the why lists security controls (filtering, rate limits, data minimisation) that belong to Input/Output/Hosting; it does not ask how value is kept up (maintenance, updates, re-checks).

rows.why: Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover from a new attack or harmful behaviour of the customer-facing AI once found.
The customer-facing AI can be quickly disabled or replaced by a fallback when it behaves outside intended use, and someone is responsible for doing so.
Incidents and errors from the customer-facing AI are communicated to affected customers and partners, tracked, and reviewed after recovery.

missing.reason: An assessor can ask whether answers given to customers are checked for bias or unequal treatment of different customers or groups; nothing in the draft covers it.

rows.why: The intended purpose, users and settings of the model the org builds or tunes, and the impact of its release on recipients, are documented.
rows.review_reason: LLM-16.1 (secure development process) is not evidence of documenting the model's intended purpose, users and settings; cis_refs off-topic.

rows.why: Requirements for the model, including safety and privacy, are elicited and drive design and tuning decisions.
The task the model supports and the methods used to build or tune it (from scratch, base model, domain tuning) are defined.
The model's knowledge limits, how its output may be used, overseen and interpreted, are documented and communicated to those who receive the model.
rows.review_reason: Folds MEASURE 2.9 but the why never asks whether the model itself is explained and validated, only limits and communication; ask it fully or give MEASURE 2.9 its own row.

rows.why: The benefits the model is meant to give recipients are examined and documented, including with the recipients themselves.
The cost to recipients of the model's errors or unsafe changes is examined and documented against the org's risk tolerance.
rows.review_reason: Cost to recipients of the model's errors repeats MAP 5.1 (likelihood and magnitude of harm to recipients from release); same check in different words.

rows.why: The scope the model is released for is specified from its capabilities, so recipients know what it should and should not be used for.
rows.review_reason: Scope the model is released for and what recipients should not use it for repeats MAP 2.2 (how output may be used, limits communicated) and MAP 1.1 (intended purpose and settings).

rows.why: The base models and software the model is built from are mapped for technical and legal risk, including IP infringement, and the internal controls applied to them are documented.
Likelihood and magnitude of harm to recipients from releasing the model are assessed, using red teaming and past incidents.
People who did not build the model, or independent assessors, take part in assessing it before and after release.
The model is shown to be valid and reliable under conditions like those of the recipients' use before release, and its limits beyond those conditions are documented.
The behaviour of the released model (API, weights, embedded) is monitored in production for drift and misuse, where the org can see it.
The model is evaluated for safety risks and shown to fail safely when operated beyond its knowledge limits.
The security and resilience of the model against adversarial attack are evaluated and documented before release.
Model build, tuning and release events are logged so changes to the model can be traced to who made them.
The model is tested for memorising or leaking personal data from its training or tuning data.
rows.review_reason: LLM-16.3 (root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities) does not support testing for memorised or leaked personal data; cis_refs off-topic.

rows.why: Bias in the model's behaviour across the groups affected by the decisions recipients make with it is evaluated before release, since recipients inherit it.
Recipients of the model have a way to report problems with it, and the reports feed into its evaluation.
Performance of new model versions is compared against a baseline so declines after tuning or release are identified and documented.
A documented decision is made on whether the model meets its purpose and should be released.
Procedures exist to respond to and recover from a previously unknown risk found in a released model.
A released model can be withdrawn, replaced or deactivated when it behaves outside its intended use, with named responsibility.
Pre-trained models and other third-party resources the build starts from are monitored and maintained, including upstream vulnerabilities and changes.
A post-release monitoring plan is implemented for the model, with scheduled re-evaluation and red teaming after release.
rows.review_reason: Empty cis_refs although LLM-8.11 (audit log reviews) supports post-release monitoring; also overlaps MEASURE 2.4 (production monitoring for drift), keep the two checks distinct.

rows.why: Updates to a released model are tested, versioned and communicated to recipients before they receive them.
Incidents and errors in the model are tracked, communicated to the recipients who depend on it, and recovered from.

notes.reason: This row and MAP 3.2, MAP 5.1 protect recipients and the people affected by their decisions (harm to people/processes); the area's impacts (assets only) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Nothing checks the experimental design, construct validation and choice of training/tuning data when the org builds or tunes the model.
Nothing checks how feedback from recipients and others affected by the model, on positive, negative and unanticipated impacts, is gathered and fed back into the build.
Training and tuning a model has an environmental and energy cost that an assessor can ask about for this area.
Nothing checks that the model's performance in recipients' real deployment contexts is validated with input from domain experts and recipients.
Nothing checks the mechanisms (retraining, support, maintenance) that sustain the value of a released model for recipients over time.

rows.why: The intended purpose and context of use of the AI's answers, and who relies on them for which decisions or actions, are understood and documented.
The limits of what the AI's answers can be trusted for, and how people and systems may use and oversee them, are documented.
rows.review_reason: The 'how people and systems may use and oversee them' part repeats MAP 3.5 (which outputs need human checking and how oversight works); keep only the knowledge limits here.

rows.why: The cost of wrong answers being trusted, and who or what could be harmed by a wrong decision or action, is examined and documented.
It is defined which outputs need a person to check them before they are acted on, and how that oversight works.
The likelihood and size of impact from steered (injection, poisoning) and inaccurate answers are assessed and documented.
The test sets, metrics and tools used to check answer quality and injection resistance are documented.
Answer quality and behaviour are monitored in production for drift, made-up facts and inconsistency, and improvements or declines over time are identified from field data and documented.
Accuracy and consistency of answers to the same question are demonstrated under conditions like real use (messy inputs, retrieved content), and the limits beyond tested conditions are documented.
The output is evaluated for what happens when it is wrong or made to go beyond its knowledge limits, and that it fails safely.
rows.review_reason: LLM-16.13 (application penetration testing) does not evidence that wrong or out-of-knowledge output fails safely, and it is already used on MEASURE 2.7; the ref is weak.

rows.why: Resistance of answers to prompt injection and poisoned content is tested, for example by red-teaming, and documented.
rows.review_reason: LLM-16.3 (root cause analysis on vulnerabilities) is not evidence for injection/poisoning resistance testing; drop it.

rows.why: Outputs are logged with what produced them, so wrong or steered answers can be traced and reviewed.
Output is presented and interpreted within its context so people can judge how far to trust it.
rows.review_reason: LLM-8.5 (detailed audit logs) does not support how output is presented and interpreted so people can judge trust; the ref is off-topic.

rows.why: The answer-quality and injection tests and metrics are themselves reviewed for whether they catch failures, so a weak test set cannot hide them.
People who receive answers can report wrong output and appeal decisions based on it, and these reports feed evaluation.
Domain experts and users validate, in the deployment context, that answers are consistently as intended, and the results are documented.
A determination is made and recorded whether the answers meet the intended purpose and whether the AI should continue to be relied on.
Mechanisms such as business rules that limit or restrict what answers can be used for, and human-AI teaming set-ups, are in place and applied to keep answers valuable and trustworthy in use.
Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover from wrong or steered output once found.
The output or AI can be switched off or bypassed when answers are inconsistent with intended use, with thresholds and owners.
Wrong-output incidents are communicated to those affected, tracked, and recorded with their fixes.

missing.reason: Nothing checks that accuracy, consistency and trust requirements for the AI's answers were elicited from the people and systems relying on them.
Nothing checks the benefit the answers are meant to bring (performance against a human baseline), which is what wrong-answer cost is weighed against.
Post-deployment plan for output (user input, appeal and override, change management when a model or prompt update changes answers) is not asked beyond drift monitoring in MEASURE 2.4.

rows.why: How training, tuning, evaluation and test sets are collected and selected (availability, representativeness, suitability) is documented, and the harness test cases are kept separate from the data the model was trained on.
The sources of third-party and licensed data used for training, tuning and testing are identified, with the rights and IP or licence risks of using them.
Third-party datasets and feedback or logs reused for tuning are reviewed for bias, privacy and poisoning risk before they enter a training, tuning or test set.
The evaluation and test sets, metrics and harness tools are documented and versioned, so a result can be traced to the exact data and test cases used.
Evaluation sets drawn from people (human-subject data, feedback) meet consent and protection requirements and represent the population the system serves.
Training and tuning sets, the evaluation set and the harness are tested and protected against poisoning and tampering, including changes made to hide failures.
Changes to and access to training, tuning and evaluation data and the harness are logged and attributable to a person, so tampering and misuse can be traced.
Personal and sensitive data in training sets and in feedback or logs reused for tuning is identified, minimised or removed, and its use is documented.
The evaluation set and harness are reviewed to confirm they still catch real failures, are refreshed, and have not been narrowed or leaked into training.
Controls on the data used for training, tuning and testing (quality, minimisation, encryption, retention, deletion on request) are applied in practice.
When poisoned or tampered training, tuning or evaluation data, or a leak from them, is found, the org responds and restores a clean, verified copy of the data and harness.

The legal and IP risks of the model's components are mapped: licence terms and provenance of base models, fine-tuning data and third-party prompts or configurations, and the risk of infringing or leaking rights in the model itself.
rows.review_reason: Licence terms and provenance of base models and fine-tuning data belong to Model building and Test, tuning and evaluation data; the Model area is the weights and versions as IP, so the why mixes in other areas' checks.

rows.why: Internal controls that protect the model artifacts (storage, access, versioning, release of weights) are identified and documented.
rows.review_reason: Repeats MANAGE 2.2 (controls on weights, versions, prompts) in different words, and only asks that controls are identified and documented; LLM-3.3 is about retrieved content and memory stores (Source data), off-topic here.

rows.why: API usage and version state are monitored in production for signs of model extraction, copying or unexpected changes to a deployed version.
The model is tested for theft, extraction through the API and tampering with versions, and the results are documented.
Access to weights, prompts and configurations, and changes to model versions, are logged so copying or tampering can be traced to who did it.
rows.review_reason: LLM-3.14 (monitor LLM logging for access to known sensitive data) does not support logging access to weights, prompts and version changes; LLM-8.5 is mostly about user inputs and outputs (Input area); LLM-8.1 or LLM-8.10 would fit better.

rows.why: Controls such as restricted access, encryption and protected backups are applied to weights, fine-tuned versions and system prompts.
rows.review_reason: LLM-3.3 is about retrieved content and memory stores (Source data), off-topic for protecting weights; LLM-6.8 (role separation for model promotion) or LLM-6.5 (MFA on model registries) would support it.

rows.why: Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover from theft, leakage or tampering of the model or its configuration.
A tampered or leaked model version can be withdrawn, rolled back to a trusted version, and access to it revoked.
What the retrieval store covers and does not cover, and the upstream data the AI depends on, is documented so users and assessors know what answers can rest on it.
rows.review_reason: Subcategory is knowledge limits and human oversight of output; the why (coverage plus upstream data) repeats MAP 4.1's source identification, with the same CIS refs LLM-3.2 and LLM-3.8.

rows.why: What content is collected into the retrieval store and how it is selected for suitability, quality and trustworthiness of source is defined and documented.
The sources feeding the retrieval store, including third-party or external content, are identified with where the data flows and the rights to use it.
Controls on the store itself are identified and documented: classification of its content, who can read or change it, and protection against tampering.
The content of the store and the answers drawn from it are monitored in production for unexpected changes, poisoned or stale material.
Retrieval permissions, poisoning and copying out of the store through the AI are tested, so users only see what they are entitled to.
Retrievals and changes to the store are logged with who asked and what was returned, so access to sensitive content can be traced.
Personal and sensitive data held in the store is identified, classified and checked for exposure through the AI.
Store content is kept current and accurate, and outdated or no longer needed material is retired or securely disposed of.
Procedures exist to respond to and recover from poisoned or leaked store content, including cleaning the store and re-indexing.
rows.review_reason: The why asks whether procedures 'exist' (a GOVERN-style existence check) rather than what is done in practice when store content is found poisoned or leaked.

rows.why: A source or the whole store can be disconnected from retrieval quickly when it is found poisoned or over-exposed, with responsibility assigned.
Changes to the store after go-live are tracked, and deletion and rectification requests reach the store and its index so removed content stops being retrieved.

notes.reason: Stale or poisoned content makes answers wrong and harms decisions and processes using them; the area's impacts (data, access) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Requirements for the store (who may see which content through the AI, privacy and entitlement expectations) are not asked anywhere; this is where retrieval entitlements are set.
Nothing checks that third-party or external content feeding the store is monitored and its risks controlled over time; MAP 4.1 only covers identification.
Nothing checks that retrieval fails safely, for example refusing rather than exposing restricted content when permission or classification checks fail or the store misbehaves.

rows.why: The outside networks, servers and upstream systems the AI's tools connect to, and how data flows to them, are documented.
The scope of what each tool can read, write and do, and the credentials it uses, is specified against what the use case needs.
The tools and MCP servers the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are identified with who runs each and what third-party software it brings.
Internal controls for each tool or MCP server (approval before use, permission limits, allowed versions) are identified and documented.
rows.review_reason: The why's 'permission limits' repeats MAP 3.3 (scope and credentials) and MANAGE 2.2 (permissions kept within bounds), and MCP-6.8 is reused in all three; narrow it to approval before use and allowed versions.

rows.why: The likelihood and size of harm from tool misuse (injected instructions, over-broad permissions, a compromised outside server) are assessed.
Tool use in production is monitored for unexpected calls, new capabilities on a known server and unusual volume.
Tools and MCP servers are tested for security, including prompt injection driving tool calls, permission abuse and a malicious or changed server.
Tool calls are logged with the credentials used and what was done, so actions can be traced and accounted for.
The privacy risk of data flowing through tools to MCP servers and outside services is examined, including what leaves and to whom.
Controls that keep tool use within bounds in practice (permissions narrower than the user's, short-lived credentials, gateway enforcement, rate limits) are applied and kept working.
A tool or MCP incident (misused credential, injected call, compromised server) has a response and recovery procedure that is followed.
A tool, credential or MCP server can be switched off or revoked quickly, with an owner assigned, when it misbehaves.
Outside MCP servers and tool suppliers are monitored regularly and their risk controls applied and documented.
Post-deployment monitoring of tools covers change management for new tools or permissions, review of use, and decommissioning of unused tools.
rows.review_reason: 'Review of use' repeats the MEASURE 2.4 check on production tool use (same MCP-8.11); keep only change management for new tools or permissions and decommissioning.

rows.why: Tool incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected, and followed up after recovery.

missing.reason: Nothing asks which tool actions (writes, deletes, payments, external sends) need a human to confirm before they run; MCP-17.4 itself mentions human confirmation enforcement.
Nothing checks that the AI fails safely when a tool or MCP server errors, times out, is unavailable or returns something unexpected, rather than retrying or taking partial changes.

rows.why: The tasks each agent performs and the chains of actions, tools and systems it uses to do them are defined and documented.
The agent's knowledge limits, the conditions outside its intended use, and how its output is used and overseen by humans are documented.
The scope of what each agent may do on its own is specified: which systems, which actions, which data, and which actions are never left to it.
Human oversight of agent actions is defined: which steps need approval or review, who does it, and how it is trained and assessed.

The components an agent is built on (models, orchestration frameworks, libraries, executors) are identified and held to approved, controlled versions, with their legal and supply-chain risks documented.
rows.review_reason: Folded MAP 4.1 is not fully asked: the why says 'legal and supply-chain risks documented' but not third-party IP/rights infringement or the inventory of third-party material; AGENT-16.4 (third-party component inventory) supports it and is missing.

rows.why: The likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions are assessed, including irreversible changes and actions triggered by manipulated input.
rows.review_reason: AGENT-16.6 is a vulnerability severity rating process, not evidence for likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions; drop it.

rows.why: Agent behaviour in production is monitored for unexpected action chains, tool use and drift from what was approved.
The agent is shown to complete its tasks correctly and reliably under realistic conditions, and the limits of where it can be trusted are documented.
rows.review_reason: Showing the agent answers correctly and reliably is accuracy/consistency TEVV, done at Output for everyone; keep only if reworded to agent task completion and limits of autonomy; empty cis_refs although AGENT-16.13 (evaluation harnesses, adversarial inputs) supports it.

rows.why: Agents are tested under stress and unexpected conditions to show they fail safely, with loops and runaway action chains stopped.
Agent security is tested with adversarial and red-team exercises, including manipulated input that triggers actions and attempts to break out of the sandbox.
Agent actions, tool calls and the identity used are logged and kept so what an agent did can be traced and reviewed.
An agent's decisions and action chains can be explained, documented and interpreted in context, so reviewers understand why it acted.
rows.review_reason: Largely repeats MEASURE 2.8 (what the agent did, traced from logs); AGENT-8.5/8.11 are the same evidence; no distinct explainability check for this area.

rows.why: Privacy risk from the data an agent reads, keeps in memory and passes between tools is examined, including redaction in logs.
rows.review_reason: Redaction in logs and the log CIS refs (AGENT-8.1, 8.5) belong to Input (prompt and response logs); privacy of data passed between tools overlaps Input, Source data and MCP/tools; the row reads as generic privacy.

rows.why: Staff and others can report agent misbehaviour and unexpected actions, and these reports feed how the agent is evaluated.
Feedback from operators and users, and how often staff override the agent, are used to judge whether it performs as intended.
Results are used to decide whether the agent achieves its purpose and whether its autonomy should continue, be reduced or be stopped.
Controls limit what an agent can do: least-privilege identities, sandboxing, approval for high-impact or irreversible steps, and limits on rate and cost.
Agent-specific incidents are responded to and recovered from, including reversing the changes an agent made.
An agent can be stopped, bypassed or its access revoked quickly when it acts outside its intended use, and who may do so is assigned.
Post-deployment monitoring of agents covers staff override, change management of agent configuration and tools, and retirement of agents.
rows.review_reason: Staff override is the same check as MEASURE 4.2 (override frequency); the why also mixes change management and retirement, so it asks several things; AGENT-8.11 log review does not support override.

rows.why: Agent incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected and reviewed for root cause.

notes.reason: The row limits rate and cost, which harms spend/assets; the area's impacts (access, process, data) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Nothing checks agent performance and assurance criteria measured under conditions like the real deployment (real systems, messy inputs, non-optimised conditions); AGENT-16.13 supports it.
Nothing asks what benefit justifies giving the agent autonomy (time saved, error rates against a human baseline) as examined with its users.

description: AI RMF mapping: per AI area, rows of AI RMF function -> subcategory, CIS safeguards that prove it, impact. Drafted and evaluated by agents (prompts/ai_rmf_mapping_*.md), recorded by record_ai_bank.py mapping, reviewed by a person. Model: AI_RMF_Mapping_Sheet_Design.md.
